en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhipan of Donghu, Siming, during the fourth year of the Jingding era of the Song Dynasty.
Part Three of the First Section: The Fundamental Chronicle of the Lord Śākyamuni Buddha.
Year twelve, *xinmao* (1231 BCE): The Buddha dispatched Maudgalyāyana to inform his father, the King, and Yaśodharā, saying: "Great..."
My son Rāhula is already nine years old;
he should now be permitted to leave the household life.
Yaśodharā replied,
"When the Tathāgata was a prince,
he took me as his wife."
"Before even three years had passed, he fled to the mountains and marshes.
After six years of arduous toil, he attained Buddhahood and returned to his kingdom.
Now, desiring to seek out my son once again—how cruel this is!—he has returned to the kingdom of Kapilavastu."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana used skillful means to instruct and enlighten him,
but [the king] had no intention at all to listen.
The World-Honored One then dispatched a manifested person who proclaimed from mid-air:
"Do you perhaps remember when you bought five stalks of lotuses for five hundred silver coins to offer to the Buddha Dīpaṃkara?
At that time, you requested of me that we be wife and husband in every lifetime,
to which I replied, 'A Bodhisattva fulfills his vows through many kalpas.'"
"In all acts of giving, I do not oppose the wishes of others.
If you can do likewise, I will accept you as my wife.
Make a vow to this effect."
"I shall follow whatever you bestow upon me and vow never to have a regretful heart;
why then do you now cherish Rāhula and prevent him from leaving the household life?
Having heard this, Yaśodharā recalled her past lives.
As he saw what had occurred yesterday,
his parental affection for his beloved son naturally subsided;
he took Rāhula by the hand and entrusted him to Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, King Śuddhodana immediately assembled the prominent clans of the kingdom and dispatched one son from each to follow my grandson.
Fifty men went to where the Buddha was;
they sent Ānanda to shave their heads,
as well as those of the fifty princes of the royal house.
He commanded Śāriputra to serve as his upādhyāya and Maudgalyāyana to serve as his ācārya.
Rāhula did not delight in hearing the Dharma.
The Buddha, for his sake, explained the unprecedented causal conditions (*adbhutadharma*).
Upon receiving the ten precepts, he immediately realized the four fruits of the śramaṇa. This is the *Adbhutadharma-sūtra*. King Śuddhodana then went to the Buddha and said:
In the past, when the Buddha first left the household life,
he still had Nanda; now that Nanda has also gone forth,
the only one upon whom his remaining affections are placed is this son.
"Now that I am about to leave the household life, my plans for the kingdom are forever ended.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma to the king to console him.
He further assembled the bhikṣus and established a regulation.

The parents did not permit or allow him to leave the household life. In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, the Buddha went to the Śītavana Grove to preach the Dharma to Daṅguma. In the *Dvādaśayātra-sūtra*, the Buddha preached the Eight Precepts of the Uposatha (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla*) to the bhikṣus. In the *Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa-śīla-sūtra*, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was a group of seventeen youths;
the eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve.
Having left the household life out of faith,
the bhikṣu immediately ordained him.
After receiving full ordination, he was unable to endure even a single meal and wept throughout the night.
The Buddha, having awakened to this, questioned and understood the matter and established the regulation:

"When one has reached twenty years of age, they should receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the Buddha ordained that the half-monthly recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) be held;
however, when the assembly gathered for it, they became fatigued.
The *Four-Part Vinaya* permits each monastery to establish its own great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).

In the thirteenth year, the *Renchen* (13 years after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa), the Buddha returned to the kingdom of Magadha and preached the *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* for King Puṣya. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Lohitya requested the establishment of a precept platform (*śīla-maṇḍala*).
To confer the full ordination upon bhikṣus,
the Buddha commanded that a *jietan* (precept altar) for the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* be established outside the eastern gate of the southern enclosure of Jetavana,
rising from the ground and marked by three tiers.
This was to symbolize the three emptinesses.
Śakra further added an inverted cauldron to cover the śarīra,
and Mahābrahmā placed a priceless jewel upon the inverted cauldron.
These constitute the five layers,
representing the Brahma-king’s precious jewel of the fivefold Dharma-body;
those with great merit and virtue see it as being as large as a five-peck jar.
Its light illuminates eight hundred *yojanas*.

Those of little merit see it as a mass of ink. According to the *Nanshan Jitan Tujing* (Illustrated Scripture of the Ordination Platform at Mount Wutai), in the fourteenth year, the *guisi* year, the Buddha went beneath the Tree of Fear (*Bhaya-vṛkṣa*).
He preached the *Benqi jing* (Sutra on Past Deeds) and the *Shieryou jing* (Sutra on the Twelve Wanderings) for Maitreya Bodhisattva.
In the fifteenth year, the Jia-wu year, the Buddha returned once more to Kapilavastu and preached the Dharma for his father, the King.

The Buddha delivered eighty-four thousand members of the Śākya clan, who attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. In the *Dvādaśayātra-sūtra*, it is recorded that when the Buddha returned to his native land,
he ascended into the air with his feet until they were level with people's heads.
He merely had his father, the King, touch his feet;
he did not wish to humble himself by distinguishing [the parents'] merit. This is precisely what it means for parents to receive reverence in return, serving as proof that it generates merit.
While this may be possible for a Buddha,
as for the bhikṣus of the final age,
their practice has become somewhat thin.

Fearing that it might not yet be appropriate to receive the profound veneration of his parents, the Buddha, for the sake of his father the King and the great assembly, preached the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.
He described how the Buddha’s body is golden in color and its radiance is immeasurable.
At that time, because of their karmic obstructions, the five hundred Śākyas perceived the Buddha’s physical body as being like a haggard, grey-skinned Brahmin.
The Buddha then preached to them regarding the sins of their past wrong views.
Now, by invoking the Buddha’s name, prostrating, and repenting, one immediately beholds the Buddha’s body, golden like Mount Sumeru.
Seeking ordination from the Buddha, one attains arhatship. This concludes the first chapter of the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, "The Buddha Returns to His Kingdom."
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Buddha’s maternal aunt, sought to leave the household life, but was refused twice.
When the Buddha returned to his native country for a second time, she again requested to become a renunciant.
As before, it was not permitted.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Mahāprajāpatī wishes with all her heart to receive the Dharma and the Vinaya."
"May the Buddha grant his permission.
The Buddha commanded that she observe the Eight Rules of Respect for as long as her life lasted.
Thereupon, Mahāprajāpatī was permitted to go forth.
In the *Biqiuni shizhong benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising of the Initial and Intermediate Events for Bhikṣuṇīs), regarding the bhikṣuṇīs receiving the Eight Rules of Respect:
first, a bhikṣuṇī of even a hundred years' standing must pay homage at the feet of a bhikṣu who has been ordained for only five summers.
Second, one must not revile or slander bhikṣus.
Third, one must not expose the faults of bhikṣus;
however, bhikṣus may speak of the faults of bhikṣuṇīs.
Fourth, a śikṣamāṇā should seek to receive the full ordination from the community of monks.
Fifth, a bhikṣuṇī who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Every half-month, one should seek out a person to provide instruction within the assembly of both divisions of the Sangha.
Seventh, one should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there are no bhikṣus. Thus the Buddha told Ānanda in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
After my parinirvāṇa,
the True Dharma shall endure for one thousand years;
because women have gone forth, it shall be reduced by five hundred years.
Later, he was taught the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
He further obtained the *Sudarśana-sūtra* and the *Dharmasthitistava*.
The commentary states:
The Tathāgata traveled through sixteen great kingdoms for twelve years,
transforming and delivering people by preaching such sūtras as the four Āgamas and the brief instructions of the seven Buddhas.
In this year, he began to preach the extensive precepts:
namely, the two hundred and fifty precepts for bhikṣus and the five hundred precepts for bhikṣuṇīs.
Since the two assemblies were disciplined according to each offense as it occurred,
the Buddha later compiled these articles and regulations as the fundamental basis for the observance of those who have left the household life.
Regarding "simultaneous with others" and so forth:
it refers to manifesting a single buddha-field such that its purity and impurity appear different,
and manifesting a single body such that its vastness and minuteness appear distinct.
When preaching the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind;
because his supernormal powers are unshared, they perceive purity and impurity,
and hear praise and censure.
Among fragrances, there are those that are *campaka* and those that are not;
among flowers, there are those that adhere to the body and those that do not;
and among wisdoms, there are those that are "as-if-thousandfold" and those that are not.

This is as explained in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* (Netting Name) and the *Vaipulya-sūtra* (Mysterious Ten), with a supplementary note stating that "thousand" (*qian*) should be read as "some" (*ruo gan*) or "ten thousand" (*ruo wan*). Regarding the pronunciation "gan," it carries no meaning. Next, the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) is discussed.
This means that one first explains the Small [Vehicle] and subsequently the Great [Vehicle].

he extracted the Great from the Small.
This causes them to sever their fetters and become noble ones (*ārya*).
Although there is this benefit, it is not the Buddha’s primary intention.
Next, he taught the Vaipulya sūtras: the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Aṅgulimālīya*.
This is called "Manifestation in All Worlds.
A son of a brahmin, twelve years of age,
was foremost among men in his physical strength and the perfection of his marks.
He addressed the Buddha with verses.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!
and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and attained arhatship;
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, the ten disciples, Mañjuśrī, and the others were all rebuked.
The Buddha said,
"In the southern direction there is a land named Sarvaratnavyuha."
There was a Buddha named Mahāvīra;
he is none other than Aṅgulimāla. The *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), fascicle 10, states: [as cited above].
The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* was preached in the sixth year [after his enlightenment]. This sūtra states that it was spoken six years after attaining enlightenment;
now the Great Master cites it as proof.

The teaching of the third period was intended for this reason and for this purpose: it rebukes the small vehicle (Hīnayāna) for its addiction to preserving fixed fruits—a fault residing primarily among the Śrāvakas—and it simultaneously censures the nihilism of the Tripiṭaka, which targets those of dull faculties who are Bodhisattvas; thus, it addresses both Śāriputra and Subhūti.
The teachings of the Qi dynasty were exclusively focused on the Hinayana;
from the beginning, they had never heard of the majestic power of the Mahayana.
Subhūti was thus bewildered and lost his bowl, as stated in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra.
Subhūti said: "In the past, when I was begging for alms, Vimalakīrti— "
He took my bowl and filled it with rice,
saying to me: "If you can be equal toward food, you shall also be equal toward all phenomena."
Since all dharmas are equal, one is also equal regarding food;
it is only by begging in this manner that one may take food.
To slander the Buddhas and destroy the Dharma [is to act otherwise].
"You shall not be counted among the multitude,
and you will ultimately not attain nirvāṇa.
Only if you act in this manner may you take this food."
At that time, World-Honored One, I heard this and was utterly bewildered;
I did not recognize what these words meant,
nor did I know how to respond.
He then set down his bowl and was about to leave the house, but Śāriputra, overcome with fear,
withdrew the flower from Vimalakīrti’s room. A goddess said to Śāriputra,
"Your fetters and habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted."
Flowers adhere to the body and ears.
As for the statement, "When the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, flowers do not adhere," it is not understood what this means.
Not knowing how to answer, he wrote on the slip:
"Since the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*) is the primary means for entering the Way, these two persons are employed as such;
thus, the teachings of the Vaipulya [sūtras] employ censure and rebuke."
Regarding the period after the Tripitaka and the time when [the Buddha] was rebuked, it should have been before the twelve years at the Deer Park—that is, prior to the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings.
As for the old tradition stating "in the middle," this must be an error. How is this known?
All of them recounted their past reproaches,
verifying that these were matters from former lives;
for they had previously received the teachings and attained the Way.
Having realized the state of no-more-learning,
they bore the Buddha’s profound kindness in their hearts and trusted one another with sincere conviction.
No longer did he feel anger;
from ancient times until now,
he had freely endured Aṅgulimāla’s insults.

He freely accepts the refutations of Vimalakīrti, gaining the benefit of feeling shame for the Small Vehicle while aspiring toward the Great; he critiques the biased and refutes the Small, sighing over the Small while praising the Perfect. (Xuan-ten: Critique of the Biased, Refutation of the Small, Sighing at the Small, Praising the Perfect. (Xuan-ten: Critique of the Biased.)
As it is said in the "Vimalakīrti-bodhisattva" chapter,
where Vimalakīrti rebukes Maitreya, saying:
"The World-Honored One has bestowed upon you, O Venerable One, a prediction [of enlightenment]."
By means of which birth is the prediction bestowed?
Is it the past, the future, or the present?
It is further said:
"All sentient beings practice the characteristics of bodhi.
If Maitreya were to enter parinirvāṇa,"
"All sentient beings shall likewise be extinguished," and it is further said:
"Bodhi cannot be attained by means of the body."
It cannot be attained through the mind.
Furthermore, the *Māra-sūtra* states:
"The Arhat Aṅgulimāla..."
It specifically excludes Mañjuśrī’s ten disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings;
this constitutes using the Perfect [Teaching] to critique the partiality of the Three Teachings and subduing the Hinayana,
as seen in the "Disciples Chapter."
Maudgalyāyana was preaching the Dharma to a layperson when Vimalakīrti rebuked him, saying:
"As for one who preaches the Dharma..."
It should be explained according to the Dharma: there are no names,
for speech has been cut off.
The Dharma is ineffable,
for it is free from applied and sustained thought;
thus, it employs the three teachings of the Mahāyāna gateway.
He refuted Maudgalyāyana’s three "inappropriatenesses":
first, that he explained outwardly according to the characteristics of dharmas while understanding inwardly according to the characteristics of dharmas.
This is because using the emptiness of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) to reject that which is not immediately empty constitutes a teaching that does not accord with the principle.
Second, there is the external understanding of faculties and conditions.
Internally possessing excellent knowledge and vision,
one attains freedom from obstruction;
for this reason, it is distinguished and refuted separately.
Third, externally one has compassionate thoughts for sentient beings,
and internally one reflects upon repaying the Buddha's kindness;
this is used to achieve perfect penetration.
Furthermore, Aṅgulimāla dismissed ten disciples;
this serves as a praise of the Great [Vehicle] by means of the three teachings of the Noble Gate, which surpasses the Small [Vehicle].
This is as explained in the "Chapter on Sentient Beings."
Just as a magician observes a person afflicted by illness,
so does a bodhisattva regard sentient beings;
it is like a wise person seeing the moon in water.
An elephant in a mirror;
a mirage in the heat of the sun—
thus does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings.
Now, to apply this analogy to sentient beings is to encompass the intent of both the Perfect and Round Teachings [to] praise the Round.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
That superior person is difficult to respond to;
they have profoundly penetrated the true nature of reality.
"He skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma. This praises Vimalakīrti.
Mañjuśrī entered Vimalakīrti’s room.
Vimalakīrti said, "Welcome,
Mañjuśrī. You have come without the characteristic of coming."
"To see by not seeing forms" is a praise of Mañjuśrī; this is taught in all four teachings.
The Tripitaka is termed the "half-character."
The Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings] constitute the "full" letters;
they are called "full" in contrast to the "half.
Thus, it is said in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the teaching: [text].
It is like a householder who has only an only son;
his heart constantly cherishes him with affection, attending to him diligently day and night,
yet he teaches him only the half-syllables and does not teach the full syllables.
This is truly because his son’s capacity was not yet sufficient; thus,
half [of the teachings] consist of the nine divisions of the Hīnayāna,
while the full [set] consists of the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding persons and principles,
this can be understood through comparison.
If one considers the time, then at the hour of eating, from the level ground, a single illumination emerges and opens out.
If considered in terms of flavor, it is like clarified butter being produced from curd.
This is derived from the *Vaipulya Sūtras*; the "Chapter on Profound Faith and Understanding" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "After this,..."
Regarding the phrase "mutually trusting the mental characteristics" (*xinxiang tixin*) and "entering and exiting without difficulty": as for "characteristics" (*xiang*), it means...
This refers to mutual trust.
It means that since one has obtained the price of nirvana through the Three Baskets (Tripitaka), this is not in vain.
Now, to speak this Mahāyāna for the sake of a bodhisattva is likewise not in vain;
this is precisely the son’s faith in his father.
The Buddha, knowing that these individuals have already severed their views and afflictions, understands that they will certainly not slander what they hear.
Possessing sharp untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they will give rise to faith upon hearing even a subtle teaching;
this is precisely like a father’s faith in his son.
Because of this, one beholds the body of sublime distinction;
hearing the teachings of the Mahāyāna is termed "entry.
Yet, when further rebuked and corrected, one still perceives only the six-foot form.
Explaining the Dharma of the Small Vehicle is called "emerging.
Whether entering or emerging from the Great or Small Vehicles, there is no doubt or difficulty. Nevertheless, their place of abiding remains as it was originally;
thus, although they enter and emerge without difficulty, they have not yet attained entry into the Mahāyāna.
They claim that this is the business of bodhisattvas and not within the scope of their own wisdom; thus,
they are unwilling to turn from the Hinayana toward the Mahayana.
It is like one who dwells as an arhat and does not say that he will attain Buddhahood in the future; what is the meaning of this summary?
It clarifies that after the Tripitaka, the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) are taught next.
Having already attained the fruit of the Path, one’s mind is characterized by embodied conviction.
Hearing the Great Name is entering; dwelling in the Lesser Name is exiting.
To be rebuked with harsh words is called "no difficulty."
Furthermore, he proceeded further into the palace;
because he beheld the great power of merit belonging to the ministers and the noble clans,
it was called "Entering."
"Emerging" refers to dwelling in the thatched huts of the two vehicles; therefore,
it is called "emerging."
Regarding "the mind's nature of trust":
having attained arhatship, one does not become angry when reviled; instead, one feels shame and remorse within the heart.
I did not dare to transform others by using the Śrāvaka branch of the Buddha-dharma. (Xuán, 10) The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states:
Ānanda said, "At that time, I was truly filled with shame and remorse."
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"Alas! I deeply reproach myself.
How could I have deceived myself? This shame is small indeed."
"I do not know how I shall attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
This expresses his aspiration for greatness;
it is the designation established by the teachings of the Vaipulya section.

Now, I shall rely on the texts of the sutras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries.
This is considered a relinquishing of that [transgression].

Desiring to be born among humans or devas;
desiring to attain the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] or the state of a pratyekabuddha;
desiring to attain Buddhahood.
All should repent to eliminate karmic obstructions and settle securely within the Vaipulya [Mahāyāna] teachings.
The Continued Record states:
"The name 'Vaipulya' has two meanings."
If the great sūtras are like the cream produced from curd,
this illustrates how the Vaipulya scriptures emerge from the Sūtras;
this refers to the third period, which is named Vaipulya.
This immediately engages the capacities of the three vehicles and the four teachings.
If the *Puxian guan* (Contemplation of Samantabhadra) is designated as a Vaipulya [sūtra],
it directly elucidates the principle of the Perfect [Teaching].
Regarding the Vaipulya scriptures cited here,
there is a concern that they might be considered identical to the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* in being named after their underlying principle;
therefore, I have cited the passages concerning the repentance of the Three Vehicles.
To establish this name definitively,
it is derived from the Vaipulya teachings of the Nikāyas, which do not exclusively focus on either phenomena (dharma) or principle (tattva).
Regarding the Vaipulya, various texts and treatises offer three explanations.
First is the matter of the source:
the Great Sūtra emerges from the *Sūtra*, the *Vaipulya*,
and the *Anantārthika-sūtra*.
Next, the Vaipulya [sūtras] are discussed. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states that "matured butter" refers to the Vaipulya sūtras which discipline and critique;
the *Guanfo Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) speaks of reading and reciting the Mahāyāna Vaipulya.

"The teachings of the Vaipulya (fangděng) are common to the Three Vehicles;
these all refer to the teachings of the third period."
Second, from the perspective of principle:
the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states that this Vaipulya sūtra is the eye of all Buddhas.
These three matters are both consistent with principle and practice.

This refers to entering the cool pond through four gates;
this is the "square.

for this name is definitively determined based on the specific teachings of that school.

In the sixteenth year, the year of Yiwei (475 CE), the Buddha was at the Āmra Grove in the city of Vaiśālī, where he preached the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra. Vaiśālī.
This is translated as "Vast, Majestic, and Pure.

Its shape resembles that of a pear;
it has many flowers but few fruits.
Vimalakīrti—here translated as "Pure Name"—is his name.
With the three defilements of delusion exhausted,
he possessed great renown;
he was the master of the Vaipulya section.
In the seventeenth year, Bingshen (177 CE), the Buddha preached the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. The sūtra states:
"In the eastern direction, there is a Buddha named Sūryacandraprabha."
There was a bodhisattva Brahmā named Siyi (Suvikrāntavikrāmin) who came here to question the Buddha.
In the eighteenth year, the *dingyou* year, the Buddha was on the summit of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea, preaching the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
Even non-Buddhists prohibit and do not permit the eating of meat;
how much less would the Tathāgata, who nurtures all beings with great compassion,
ever permit himself or others to eat meat?
The Buddha replied to the Bodhisattva:
"There are immeasurable causes and conditions for which one should not eat meat.
That is to say, all sentient beings have, from the very beginning,"
Through the succession of causes and conditions, one has always been a relative;
because they have been kin, one should not eat meat.
Because it grows from impure elements, one should not eat meat.
When sentient beings smell the odor [of meat], they all give rise to fear, just as a *caṇḍāla* should not eat meat.
Furthermore, one should not eat meat because it causes various incantations and arts to fail. According to the *Huayan chao*, it says: [text follows].
Mount Laṅkā is the abode of the yakṣa Rāvaṇa;
here it is called "The Inaccessible."
Only those possessing supernormal powers can reach it.
*Abhyantara* is translated here as "entering by way of roaming."
This refers to the Buddha and his great assembly crossing to the other shore of the ocean and accepting the invitation of the Yakṣa King;
they ascended into the air and departed. (The *Shiqian* states:)
If, within the Mahāyāna,
this teaching were made at the very beginning when the Brahmajāla Sūtra had already established its prohibitions.
One should know that the *Laṅkāvatāra* follows the four Āgamas and marks the beginning of the gradual prohibition; therein,
the Buddha answers the Bodhisattvas that they should not eat meat.
Thus we know that it still exists within the opening of the Hīnayāna teachings.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*— *śūraṅgama* being translated here as "heroic aspect" (*jiànxiàng*).
